habitat: Pairs and small parties in forest, forested kloofs, fynbos, succulent scrub and well-wooded gardens. In the north it is confined to montane forest.
summary: A common near-endemic resident, and the most heavily marked batis. The male has a very broad black breast-band and rufous flanks. The female has a rich rufous breast-band, throat and flanks. Both have rufous wing coverts. The eyes are yellow when not breeding. The breeding eye colour was not described. The alarm is a grinding prrritt, prrritt, prrritt. Other calls are a monotonous keep, keep, keep, a grating WEE-warrawarra, and a soft foo-foo-foo-foo. The Kemp code VB was left unchanged.

similar.note: Chinspot Batis is the dry-country bird. Its male lacks rufous, and the female’s rufous is a chin-spot and breast-band with white flanks, not rufous flanks and wing coverts.

research.note: Newman calls it a common near-endemic resident, and Avibase does not mark the Kruger occurrence rare or accidental, so status is resident and all twelve months are listed. The Kemp code is VB, a visiting breeder, and that code was left unchanged, which is why this needs review. The eyes are yellow only when not breeding. The breeding eye colour was not described. The immature is only the family note that it is a dull version of the adult. Bill and leg colours were not given. Only one allowed Kruger photograph was found, a female front in Ehlanzeni under CC BY-NC 4.0. The male side is from Betty’s Bay, the male front from the Garden Route, and the back from the Eden district. No flight photograph and no grade A Kruger recording were found. The grade A call is from Hillcrest, KwaZulu-Natal. Population figures and the Kemp code VB were left unchanged.
